title: dbt Lineage: Staging Views to the wh_gold Star Schema
purpose: Trace dbt's model lineage from silver staging views through dimension and incremental fact models to the wh_gold star schema Direct Lake serves, including the one SCD Type 2 dimension in an otherwise Type 1 gold layer.
accessibleSummary: A flow diagram tracing dbt model lineage. Two staging views, stg_positions and stg_returns, read silver Delta sources in the lakehouse. Three dimension models — dim_date, dim_portfolio, dim_benchmark — and one SCD Type 2 dimension, dim_instrument, build from those staging views. Four incremental fact models — fact_positions, fact_returns_daily, fact_risk_measures, fact_transactions — join the staging views to the dimensions. All four facts converge on the wh_gold star schema, which Direct Lake serves to Power BI. A warning node calls out the one dimension using SCD Type 2 history against three that overwrite in place, and the adapter limitation that makes dbt's incremental MERGE work on Fabric Warehouse at all.
longDescription: This is dbt's own model lineage rendered as a diagram, not a generic ETL flow. Two staging views (stg_positions, stg_returns) read silver Delta sources from the lh_analytics lakehouse using dbt's three-part cross-database source names. From those staging views, three ordinary dimension models build (dim_date, dim_portfolio, dim_benchmark) and one dimension, dim_instrument, is built as SCD Type 2 to preserve full history of changing instrument attributes — the warning node explains why this one dimension differs from its siblings and what breaks if it doesn't. Four incremental fact models build on top: fact_positions, fact_returns_daily, fact_risk_measures, and fact_transactions, each joining the staging views to the relevant dimensions and using dbt's incremental merge strategy to avoid a full rebuild every run. All four facts converge into the wh_gold star schema, which Power BI reads through Direct Lake. A second fact node explains the adapter mechanics that make the incremental merge actually work against Fabric Warehouse's T-SQL surface.

nodes.label: stg_positions (staging view)
nodes.summary: A dbt staging view reading silver positions from the lakehouse via a three-part source name.
nodes.detail: stg_positions is a dbt view model that reads lh_analytics.silver.positions using dbt's sources.yml declaration, taking advantage of cross-database T-SQL to combine the warehouse and lakehouse in one query with zero data duplication.
nodes.whyItMatters: Staging views are the single place column renames, type casts, and light cleanup happen before any dimension or fact model touches the data — every downstream model reads this normalized shape, not raw silver.

evidence.note: Cross-database queries let a single T-SQL statement combine multiple Fabric data sources in the workspace with zero data duplication.

processing: dbt source() reference resolves via sources.yml to the three-part cross-database name
Light column renaming/casting, no aggregation
outputs: stg_positions view, the single read point for all downstream position-related models
drill.example: A downstream fact model references ref('stg_positions') rather than the raw silver table directly, so a later rename of the silver column only needs a fix in one staging model.
failureModes: Downstream models bypassing the staging view and querying silver directly, duplicating cleanup logic and drifting out of sync

nodes.label: stg_returns (staging view)
nodes.summary: A dbt staging view reading silver daily returns from the lakehouse.
nodes.detail: stg_returns reads lh_analytics.silver.returns_daily the same way stg_positions reads positions — a thin view over the cross-database source, feeding fact_returns_daily and fact_risk_measures.
nodes.whyItMatters: Keeping returns staged separately from positions lets the two fact lineages (position-based and return-based) evolve independently even though both eventually join the same portfolio and date dimensions.

evidence.note: Cross-database queries let a single T-SQL statement combine multiple Fabric data sources in the workspace with zero data duplication.

processing: dbt source() reference resolves via sources.yml
Light column renaming/casting
outputs: stg_returns view feeding fact_returns_daily and fact_risk_measures
drill.example: A benchmark-return column added to silver later only requires exposing it in stg_returns for both dependent fact models to gain it.
failureModes: Silent silver schema drift not caught until a downstream fact model's test fails, rather than at the staging layer

nodes.label: dim_date
nodes.summary: A conventional calendar dimension joined by every fact model.
nodes.detail: dim_date is a standard, Type 1, generated calendar dimension providing date keys and attributes (fiscal period, trading-day flag, etc.) that every fact model in the star schema joins to.
nodes.whyItMatters: A shared, conformed date dimension is what lets facts at different grains (daily positions, daily returns) be compared and rolled up consistently by period.

inputs: A generated date spine covering the reporting horizon
processing: Derive fiscal period, trading-day flags, and other calendar attributes per date
outputs: dim_date, joined by every fact model
drill.example: fact_positions_daily and fact_returns_daily both join dim_date on position_date/return_date, letting a single report compare positions and returns for the same trading day.
controls: Reporting horizon (start/end date) the spine covers
failureModes: A fact's date column falling outside the generated spine's range, producing an unmatched join with no error

nodes.label: dim_portfolio
nodes.summary: A conformed portfolio dimension built from stg_positions, joined by every fact.
nodes.detail: dim_portfolio is a Type 1 dimension (overwrite in place, no history) built from the distinct portfolios seen in stg_positions, giving every fact model a single conformed portfolio key.
nodes.whyItMatters: Every fact in this star schema is ultimately a portfolio-level measure, so a conformed portfolio dimension is what lets a single report join facts across positions, returns, risk, and transactions consistently.

processing: Deduplicate to one row per portfolio_id
Overwrite attributes in place on change (Type 1, no history)
outputs: dim_portfolio, joined by fact_positions, fact_returns_daily, fact_risk_measures, and fact_transactions
drill.example: A portfolio's name changes after a rebrand; dim_portfolio overwrites the old name, so historical facts now display under the new name too — the explicit Type 1 trade-off this dimension makes.
controls: Choosing Type 1 (overwrite) rather than tracking portfolio-attribute history
failureModes: Needing historical portfolio names/attributes for an audit and discovering Type 1 already overwrote them — the case the SCD Type 2 warning node contrasts against

nodes.label: dim_benchmark
nodes.summary: A conformed benchmark dimension built from stg_returns, joined by return and risk facts.
nodes.detail: dim_benchmark is a Type 1 dimension built from the distinct benchmarks referenced in stg_returns, giving fact_returns_daily and fact_risk_measures a conformed benchmark key for attribution and relative-performance measures.
nodes.whyItMatters: Performance and risk measures are frequently expressed relative to a benchmark; a conformed benchmark dimension lets those comparisons join consistently rather than each fact model encoding its own benchmark logic.

processing: Deduplicate to one row per benchmark
Overwrite attributes in place on change
outputs: dim_benchmark, joined by fact_returns_daily and fact_risk_measures
drill.example: fact_returns_daily joins dim_benchmark to compute a portfolio's return relative to its assigned benchmark for a given trading day.
controls: Which benchmark identifier is treated as the conformed key across sources
failureModes: A portfolio's benchmark reassignment mid-period being applied retroactively under Type 1 overwrite, silently changing historical relative-performance figures

nodes.label: dim_instrument (SCD Type 2)
nodes.summary: The one dimension in gold that preserves full attribute history via SCD Type 2.
nodes.detail: dim_instrument is built as a Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2, closing and end-dating an existing row when a tracked instrument attribute changes (e.g. sector reclassification, rating change) and inserting a new current row — unlike the other three dimensions, which overwrite in place.
nodes.whyItMatters: Instrument attributes like sector or credit rating change over an instrument's life, and risk/performance attribution needs to know what the attribute was at the time of each historical position or transaction, not what it is today.

inputs: Distinct instrument records and their attributes from stg_positions
processing: On a tracked-attribute change, end-date the existing current row and insert a new row with an open effective-from date
Non-tracked attributes update in place as Type 1 columns within the same table
outputs: dim_instrument with full point-in-time history for tracked attributes, joined by facts using an effective-dated key
drill.example: An instrument's sector reclassification is captured as a new dim_instrument row; a report as of last quarter still joins to the sector value that was current then, not today's.
controls: Which instrument attributes are tracked (Type 2) versus overwritten (Type 1) within the same table
failureModes: See the SCD Type 2 consistency warning node — mixing Type 1 and Type 2 columns in one table is easy to get wrong at merge time

nodes.label: SCD Type 2 only on one dimension
nodes.summary: Mixing one Type 2 dimension with three Type 1 dimensions in the same gold layer is a real design tension to manage deliberately.
nodes.detail: dim_instrument alone carries full attribute history while dim_portfolio, dim_date, and dim_benchmark overwrite in place. This is a deliberate choice, not an oversight — instrument attributes are what risk attribution needs point-in-time for — but it means facts joining to dim_instrument must use an effective-dated key, while the same facts joining to the other three dimensions use a simple current-state key. Getting this join logic inconsistent across fact models is a genuine trap.
nodes.whyItMatters: A fact model that joins dim_instrument on the wrong key (current-state instead of effective-dated) silently attributes historical risk to today's instrument classification instead of the classification that was true at the time — a quiet correctness bug, not a crash.

inputs: Fact models joining both a Type 2 dimension (dim_instrument) and Type 1 dimensions in the same query
processing: Correct joins use dim_instrument's effective-dated key matched against the fact's transaction/position date
Incorrect joins use dim_instrument's surrogate key naively, matching only the current row
outputs: Either point-in-time-correct risk/performance attribution, or silently mis-attributed historical figures
drill.example: fact_risk_measures joins dim_instrument on instrument_id alone instead of an effective-dated join; every historical VaR calculation ends up attributed to whatever sector the instrument is classified as today, not the sector at calculation time.
controls: A written, tested join convention for every fact model that touches dim_instrument
dbt tests asserting no fact row's date falls outside its matched dim_instrument row's effective range
failureModes: A new fact model added later without following the effective-dated join convention, since nothing in the schema enforces it structurally
Reviewers not catching the join-key inconsistency because the query still returns rows — it just returns the wrong ones

nodes.label: fact_positions (incremental)
nodes.summary: Daily position holdings by portfolio and instrument, built incrementally.
nodes.detail: fact_positions joins stg_positions to dim_portfolio, dim_instrument, and dim_date, materialized as a dbt incremental model using a merge strategy keyed on portfolio, instrument, and date so each run only processes new/changed positions rather than rebuilding the whole fact.
nodes.whyItMatters: Position history for an investment book can be large; incremental materialization keeps the nightly dbt build fast as the fact table grows, instead of a full rebuild every run.

evidence.note: The dbt-fabric adapter implements certain T-SQL operations dbt models rely on — including behaviors equivalent to MERGE — by translating them into CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) plus DROP/CREATE sequences, because Fabric Data Warehouse's T-SQL surface does not support the same command set as SQL Server.

inputs: stg_positions joined to dim_portfolio, dim_instrument (effective-dated), and dim_date
processing: dbt incremental materialization filters to rows newer than the fact's current max date on each run
Merge strategy applies new/changed rows without a full table rebuild
drill.example: A nightly run only processes yesterday's new position rows rather than reprocessing years of history, keeping the dbt build time roughly constant as the table grows.
controls: The incremental filter's watermark column and grain
failureModes: An incremental filter based on the wrong watermark column silently skipping late-arriving position corrections

nodes.label: fact_returns_daily (incremental)
nodes.summary: Daily time-weighted returns by portfolio, joined to benchmark and date.
nodes.detail: fact_returns_daily joins stg_returns to dim_portfolio, dim_benchmark, and dim_date, built incrementally like fact_positions, providing the base return series performance attribution builds on.
nodes.whyItMatters: Daily returns are the foundation performance measurement and attribution reports are built from — every downstream return calculation traces back to this fact.

evidence.note: The dbt-fabric adapter translates dbt's incremental MERGE behavior into CTAS plus DROP/CREATE sequences to work around Fabric Warehouse's T-SQL surface limitations relative to SQL Server.

inputs: stg_returns joined to dim_portfolio, dim_benchmark, and dim_date
processing: Incremental filter processes only new daily return records each run
outputs: fact_returns_daily, the base series for performance attribution
drill.example: A quarterly attribution report aggregates fact_returns_daily over the period, joined to dim_benchmark to compute relative performance.
controls: Return calculation methodology upstream in silver, not redefined here
failureModes: A benchmark reassignment (see dim_benchmark's failure mode) propagating into historical attribution via the Type 1 join

nodes.label: fact_risk_measures (incremental)
nodes.summary: VaR, exposures, and sensitivities by portfolio and instrument, joined via the effective-dated instrument key.
nodes.detail: fact_risk_measures joins stg_returns-derived risk calculations to dim_portfolio, the effective-dated dim_instrument, and dim_date, carrying a measure_type degenerate dimension (VaR/exposure/sensitivity/stress) rather than a fourth join table.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the fact model where the SCD Type 2 join warning matters most in practice — risk attribution is specifically about what an instrument's classification was at calculation time.

evidence.note: The dbt-fabric adapter implements MERGE-equivalent behavior via CTAS plus DROP/CREATE because Fabric Data Warehouse's T-SQL surface does not support the same command set as SQL Server.

inputs: Risk calculation records joined to dim_portfolio, dim_instrument (effective-dated), dim_date
processing: Incremental merge processes new risk measures per run
measure_type distinguishes VaR/exposure/sensitivity/stress within one table instead of four
outputs: fact_risk_measures, the source for VaR dashboards and exposure reports
drill.example: A VaR calculation from three months ago still joins to the instrument's sector classification as it was three months ago, because the join uses dim_instrument's effective-dated key correctly.
controls: The effective-dated join convention (see the SCD Type 2 warning node)
failureModes: The exact silent mis-attribution failure mode described in the SCD Type 2 warning node — this is the fact model most exposed to it

nodes.label: fact_transactions (incremental)
nodes.summary: Buys, sells, corporate actions, and cash flows, keyed by source system and transaction id.
nodes.detail: fact_transactions joins transaction records to dim_portfolio, dim_instrument, and dim_date, materialized incrementally and keyed on (source_system, transaction_id) rather than a date-based watermark, since transactions can arrive out of order relative to their transaction date.
nodes.whyItMatters: Transaction history is the audit trail for portfolio accounting; getting the incremental key wrong (missing late-arriving or corrected transactions) directly corrupts that audit trail.

evidence.note: The dbt-fabric adapter's MERGE-equivalent behavior via CTAS plus DROP/CREATE is what makes dbt's incremental strategy work against Fabric Warehouse at all, given the T-SQL surface gap versus SQL Server.

inputs: Transaction records joined to dim_portfolio, dim_instrument, and dim_date
processing: Incremental merge keyed on (source_system, transaction_id), not a date watermark
New and corrected transactions merge in on each run
outputs: fact_transactions, the transaction-level audit trail in gold
drill.example: A corrected trade booked two days after the original transaction date still merges correctly into fact_transactions because the incremental key is the transaction id, not the transaction date.
controls: The (source_system, transaction_id) incremental key choice, deliberately not date-based
failureModes: Using a date-based incremental filter instead of the transaction-id key would silently drop out-of-order corrections — the reason this fact model's key differs from the others

nodes.label: wh_gold star schema
nodes.summary: The published gold layer: four facts joined to conformed dimensions in the warehouse.
nodes.detail: All four fact models converge into wh_gold, a conventional star schema where each fact joins dim_portfolio, dim_instrument, and dim_date (plus dim_benchmark for returns/risk), served to consumers through the warehouse's T-SQL surface and, for BI, through Direct Lake.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the stable, queryable contract downstream consumers build on — Power BI, ad hoc T-SQL analysis, and any future model all read this same conformed star rather than re-deriving it from silver.

evidence.note: Fabric Data Warehouse is an enterprise-scale relational warehouse built on a data lake foundation, aimed at star/snowflake schemas, curated corporate data marts, and governed semantic models for BI.

inputs: fact_positions, fact_returns_daily, fact_risk_measures, fact_transactions, and all five dimensions
processing: dbt test runs uniqueness/not-null tests on facts as a build gate
No further transformation here — this is the published state
outputs: A governed star schema in wh_gold, queryable via T-SQL or served through Direct Lake
drill.example: A single T-SQL query joins fact_risk_measures to fact_returns_daily via dim_portfolio and dim_date to compare risk-adjusted returns for a book, without touching silver at all.
controls: dbt test coverage as the quality gate before a build is considered complete
Access grants scoping who can query wh_gold directly vs only through the semantic model
failureModes: A downstream consumer bypassing the semantic model and running unbounded ad hoc queries directly against wh_gold, competing with the nightly dbt build for warehouse compute

walkthrough.title: 1. Staging: read silver once, per entity
walkthrough.explanation: stg_positions and stg_returns are the single read point over silver for every downstream model, using cross-database T-SQL with zero duplication.

walkthrough.title: 2. Three Type 1 dimensions build first
walkthrough.explanation: dim_portfolio, dim_date, and dim_benchmark overwrite in place — the conventional shape for reference data that doesn't need history.

walkthrough.title: 3. One dimension carries full history
walkthrough.explanation: dim_instrument alone is SCD Type 2, because risk attribution needs to know an instrument's classification at the time, not today.

walkthrough.title: 4. The trap: inconsistent join keys across facts
walkthrough.explanation: Mixing one Type 2 dimension with three Type 1 dimensions means fact models must use different join conventions for each — getting this wrong silently mis-attributes history.

walkthrough.title: 5. Four incremental facts build on the dimensions
walkthrough.explanation: fact_positions, fact_returns_daily, fact_risk_measures, and fact_transactions each join staging views to the dimensions, materialized incrementally so nightly builds stay fast.

walkthrough.title: 6. Risk measures are where the SCD Type 2 join matters most
walkthrough.explanation: fact_risk_measures joins dim_instrument via its effective-dated key — getting this join wrong is exactly the failure mode the warning node describes.

walkthrough.title: 7. Convergence: the published star schema
walkthrough.explanation: All four facts converge into wh_gold, the stable contract Power BI and any T-SQL consumer builds on.
